intro: A dying woman dreams that she is dancing: this waltz began as theatre music, not a ballroom miniature. Judith Bokor’s 1925 recording gives the orchestral melody to cello with piano accompaniment.
question: How can a waltz keep its pulse while its melody stretches?

relations.label: The opening waltz returns quietly
relations.basis: The opening waltz links the contrasting waltzes and is recalled in the quieter central stretch of this cello-and-piano arrangement. That recurring role is described by Richard Dyer at https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste; the later excerpt lies in the withdrawal marked near 132 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.926, sustained 14 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 143 s (cache/form/sibelius-valse-triste.txt, candidate 4; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A dance in three
cues.text: Across the opening, listen for the three-beat accompaniment beneath the cello’s longer phrases. A waltz supplies a regular step, but the melody need not stop at each bar line; the arrangement separates the two roles between cello and piano.
cues.evidence: The score establishes the waltz metre and the source identifies the cello-and-piano arrangement. The recording’s quiet opening grows around 0:10–0:15; no individual entrance is being timed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The partner is Death
cues.text: Sibelius wrote the music in 1903 for Kuolema, a play by his brother-in-law Arvid Järnefelt. In the scene behind this waltz, an old woman dreams of a masked ball; her partner turns out to be Death.
cues.evidence: Richard Dyer’s Boston Symphony note documents the play and its scene: https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste

cues.title: The passage gains weight
cues.text: The surrounding phrases gain weight compared with the restrained opening. Keep the accompaniment in mind: the dance pulse and the melodic swell are separate things, so a louder phrase need not mean a faster step.
cues.evidence: The report shows a rise in relative level around 1:05–1:15, followed by a generally fuller span. No tempo change or individual cello gesture is inferred from the attack detector.

cues.title: A home outside Helsinki
cues.text: Sibelius and his family moved to Ainola in autumn 1904, the year this waltz appeared separately in print. Lars Sonck designed the house near Lake Tuusula, where an established community of artists already lived.
cues.evidence: Ainola’s museum documents the house, architect and move: https://www.ainola.fi/ainolas-architecture-and-construction/ . The publication year is given by the Boston Symphony work note.

cues.title: The dance draws back
cues.text: The middle span draws back after the preceding build. Listen for how the dance remains recognisable at a reduced scale, without assuming that quieter phrases must keep the same momentum.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls sharply around 2:10, and the span through about 2:40 remains quieter. A strong measured change around 2:12 supports the broad contrast, not an exact phrase boundary.

cues.title: From stage to concert
cues.text: Sibelius conducted the concert premiere in Helsinki on 25 April 1904. Separate publication made a number from the play available as an independent piece; its original title had been Valse lente, “Slow waltz”.
cues.evidence: The premiere, publication and earlier title are documented in Dyer’s Boston Symphony note: https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste

cues.title: The late expansion
cues.text: The later dance includes the recording’s largest swell. Compare the accumulated weight with the opening’s restrained phrases, and listen across the sustained expansion towards the eventual withdrawal.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises after about 2:42 and reaches its highest five-second windows around 3:15–3:20, remaining comparatively high through 3:50. This is a comparison within this transfer.

cues.title: Leaving the dance
cues.text: The closing passage withdraws towards a quiet chordal postlude. Listen for the remaining resonance rather than expecting a forceful ballroom flourish at the end.
cues.evidence: Dyer describes the score’s quiet postlude. Relative level recedes around 3:55–4:20 in this arrangement, supporting the closing span without locating each chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The waltz loses weight, not its pulse
transitions.how: The fuller dance contracts into quieter, more separated gestures. In this cello-and-piano arrangement, the piano’s bass-and-chord pattern still defines the three-beat waltz while the cello’s longer notes become more exposed. Sibelius can recall the opening’s hesitant manner without introducing a new metre or an unrelated tune. Listen for the accompaniment continuing beneath the release of the melodic phrase: less weight at the join does not mean that the dance has stopped.
transitions.evidence: The draw-back boundary is 2:12, the strongest measured change, following a sharp fall in relative level around 2:05–2:10. The score’s linked waltz ideas and recurring opening manner support the explanation; the arrangement assigns the audible layers to cello and piano. Surface noise and uncertain transfer pitch prevent a dependable chord-by-chord tonal route.

transitions.title: The returning rhythm gathers a new dance
transitions.how: The quiet opening-related material becomes the means of starting again. The piano makes the waltz’s bass and following chords more continuous, and the cello’s line expands above them; short links grow into a sustained dance phrase. Sibelius preserves the three-beat framework while increasing the pressure within it. The seam is therefore heard as a familiar rhythmic gesture acquiring weight and continuity, not as a cut to an independent melody or a change from one ensemble to another.
transitions.evidence: The renewed-movement marker is 2:42, a strong measured boundary; level and attacks increase around 2:45–2:50. A provisional unshifted relation connects 0:08–0:22 with 2:31–2:45, supporting opening-related material across this join. The score supplies the continuity between waltz ideas. Neither a precise tempo change nor a local key is inferred from the noisy feature report.

transitions.title: The dance contracts into its closing chords
transitions.how: The dance’s renewed force is removed rather than answered by another full tune. Fragments of the opening manner return, the cello’s sustained line becomes shorter and more exposed, and the piano separates the remaining gestures. Sibelius reduces the waltz to a quiet three-chord postlude: harmonic punctuation outlasts the dancing phrase. In this arrangement the change is between melodic line, keyboard support and their diminishing resonance, not the withdrawal of sections of the original orchestra.
transitions.evidence: The final-withdrawal marker is 3:58, a measured boundary, followed by sustained level reduction through 4:20. The opening’s linking role and the three-chord postlude are described in Richard Dyer’s score-based note at https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste. The recorded forces are cello and piano; the uncertain transfer does not justify naming exact sounding closing chords.

facts: Helsinki with Martin Wegelius, 1885–89 · Berlin with Albert Becker · Vienna with Robert Fuchs and Karl Goldmark
Ainola, designed by Lars Sonck near Lake Tuusula; the family moved there in 1904
Swedish at home; Finnish education and Finnish texts in Kullervo and Luonnotar
Seven numbered symphonies; violin concerto; tone poems, incidental music, songs and chamber works
composer.background:
Sibelius was born in 1865 in Hämeenlinna, when Finland was an autonomous grand duchy within the Russian Empire. His family spoke Swedish, but he attended a Finnish-language school and encountered the Kalevala, Elias Lönnrot’s compilation of traditional epic poetry, in Finnish. The later national figure grew up between these cultures. His father, a doctor, died in 1868. Violin playing became the young Sibelius’s principal musical ambition, and family chamber music gave him an early practical knowledge of strings. He adopted the French form Jean from the visiting cards of a deceased uncle, replacing the familiar Janne professionally.

He entered the Helsinki Music Institute in 1885 after briefly beginning law studies. Martin Wegelius taught him composition; Ferruccio Busoni, then teaching piano in Helsinki, became a friend. Further study with Albert Becker in Berlin and Robert Fuchs and Karl Goldmark in Vienna extended his knowledge of Continental music. His hope of becoming a professional violin virtuoso did not survive an unsuccessful Vienna audition. The instrument nevertheless remained central to his melodic imagination: sustained notes against tremolando strings, rapid changes of register and the tension of a long line across the bow recur throughout the orchestral works.
composer.born: 8 December 1865, Hämeenlinna, Grand Duchy of Finland
composer.epithet: A symphonist who let small figures gather into themes and movements change shape while their underlying pulse continued.
